Here's a survey of the established solution families, ordered from simplest to most expressive. Since you specifically have *same-size per-channel embeddings* and want a **fixed-size joint embedding** regardless of channel count, the relevant mechanisms all share one idea: **treat the channel axis as a set** and reduce it with a function that is agnostic to its cardinality.

---

## The core framing: channels as a set

If your per-channel embedding is `E_c ∈ R^D` (one vector per channel at a given spatial location/patch), you want `f({E_1..E_C}) → R^D` that works for any `C`. Any valid `f` should ideally be **permutation-invariant** w.r.t. channel order (so the model isn't order-sensitive) yet still **channel-aware** (so it can tell a red from a near-IR channel). Everything below is a variant of "encode each channel → aggregate the set → re-embed," with different aggregation and channel-identity schemes.

---

## Family A — Deep Sets / permutation-invariant pooling (sum, mean, max)

The classic recipe (Zaheer et al., "Deep Sets") is `f(S) = ρ( Σ_{c∈S} φ(E_c) )`. The aggregation is `sum / mean / max`, so the output dimension is fixed regardless of `C`.

Concrete image-domain uses:

- **IFANI** (General Image Fusion for an Arbitrary Number of Inputs, PMC9002723) applies a **shared conv to each input, then max-pooling across the N inputs** to get a single salient feature map, which is concatenated back to each branch. The permutation-invariance from the symmetric max-pool is exactly what lets it take an arbitrary, unordered number of inputs.
- **Deep Multi-Modal Sets** (ar5iv 2003.01607) formalizes modality/channel collections as sets to guarantee invariance to both permutation and cardinality.

**Pros:** trivial, cheap, dimension-stable, order-invariant. **Cons:** a plain mean/max treats all channels with equal (data-independent) weight — it can't learn that channel *c* matters more for *this* sample.

---

## Family B — Attention-based pooling over channels (the workhorse)

This is the most common modern answer to your exact problem: a **learnable query (or queries) cross-attends over the set of channel embeddings**, producing a fixed number of output vectors of size `D`.

**`joint = MHA(query=Q, key=K, value=V)` where K,V are the per-channel embeddings.** With one query token you collapse `(C, D) → (1, D)`; with `k` queries you get `(k, D)` (Pooling by Multihead Attention, "PMA," from Set Transformer — see SetONet arxiv 2505.04738, which reports attention pooling beats mean/sum especially under variable/drop-off configurations, ~5× lower error).

Concrete architectures:

- **ChannelViT** (arxiv 2309.16108) — patchifies **each channel separately** with a **channel-tied linear projection**, then adds a learnable **channel embedding `chn_c`** plus a **shared positional embedding**. Treating the channel dimension as the sequence dimension means the architecture "seamlessly handles inputs with varying sets of channels." Their ablation shows channel identity embeddings are critical (removing/mean-averaging them tanks performance). They also introduce **Hierarchical Channel Sampling (HCS)** for training robustness to unseen channel subsets.
- **ChAda-ViT** (arxiv 2311.15264) — designed explicitly for **arbitrary number, order, and type of channels** (1–10 microscopy channels). Uses an **Inter-Channel Attention** on top of spatial attention, with **channel embeddings + shared positional embeddings**, and a **padding-and-masking** scheme to standardize variable channel counts into a fixed sequence (NLP-style mask excludes pad tokens from attention).
- **Panopticon** (arxiv 2503.10845) — "**attention over channels as patch embedding**." Each channel goes through a shared 2D conv; the per-channel features become **keys/values for a cross-attention with a learned query**, reducing arbitrary `{c_i}` to a fixed `P² × D`. Spectral identity is injected via **wavelength positional encodings** on the keys/values.
- **Flex** (Emerging Flexible Designs for Geospatial MMFMs, alphaxiv 2606.12595) — tokenizes each channel independently to `(C×L, D)`, then an **early-fusion cross-attention aggregates across the C channels per spatial token**, guided by learnable channel embeddings, "reducing the sequence back to `(L, D)`… can accommodate any number of channels by simply adding or removing learnable embeddings."
- **Perceiver / Perceiver IO** (arxiv 2103.03206, 2107.14795) — the general version of this pattern: a cross-attention **latent bottleneck** maps an arbitrary input array to a fixed latent set, decoupling computation from input cardinality (pad inputs with modality-specific embeddings).
- **AnySat** (arxiv 2412.14123) / **OmniSat** — a **modality-combiner** that runs self-attention over modality tokens then a **cross-attention block** with a shared learned value token to merge an arbitrary set of modalities/channels into one embedding per patch.

**Why this is the right default:** the joint embedding stays `D`-dimensional no matter how many channels you feed, aggregation weights are **data-dependent** (unlike mean pooling), and channel identity is preserved through additive **channel embeddings** (learnable ID or metadata-derived).

Sketch:

```python
# per-channel embeddings: E [B, C, D], channel_ids: [B, C]
E = E + channel_embed(channel_ids)          # channel identity (learnable or wavelength PE)
K = V = E
Q = learned_queries.expand(B, k, D)         # k=1 for single joint embedding
joint = CrossAttention(Q, K, V, mask)       # [B, k, D]  -> fixed size, any C
# optionally add channel-tied per-channel projection before this
```

---

## Family C — Hypernetwork / dynamic-weight conditioning

Instead of aggregating channel tokens, these **generate the embedding weights from channel metadata**, so channel count never enters the embedding dimension at all.

- **DOFA** (arxiv 2403.15356) — a **wavelength-conditioned dynamic hypernetwork**: it positional-encodes each band's central wavelength and generates the patch-embedding conv weights on the fly. "The patch embedding layer achieves independence from the number of spectral bands." Works for **any number of input channels**, including unseen sensors (via weight-space interpolation). Code: github.com/zhu-xlab/DOFA.
- **HyperFree / HyperVision** (arxiv 2605.17286) — "**wavelengths as lookup keys**": a learned weight dictionary over the spectrum is assembled per-input, turning arbitrary channel configs into a **unified, fixed-length token sequence**. No structural change or retraining when channels change.

**Pros:** elegant, physically grounded, zero-padding-free, generalizes to new bands. **Cons:** needs meaningful channel metadata (wavelength etc.), and you must treat metadata-less channels specially (DOFA assigns default RGB wavelengths).

---

## Practical design decisions (apply across families)

1. **Channel identity is non-negotiable.** All sources (ChannelViT ablation, ChAda-ViT, Panopticon, AnySat) inject channel identity via additive embeddings — **learnable IDs** for fixed known channels, or **metadata-derived positional encodings** (wavelength/mode) for open-ended channels. Averaging them away destroys performance.
2. **Tie the per-channel projection across channels.** ChannelViT finds **shared/tied linear filters outperform untied** ones — low-level filters transfer across channels, and tying improves robustness to varying channel sets.
3. **Handle variable counts two ways:** (a) **pad + mask** into a fixed max length (ChAda-ViT, Panopticon), or (b) use **count-agnostic pooling** (attention/Deep Sets) so no padding is needed. Attention pooling is preferable when channel sets vary a lot.
4. **Regularize for partial/unseen channel subsets during training** — HCS (ChannelViT) samples the *number* of channels uniformly then a combination, giving an unbiased distribution over `m`; this dramatically improves test-time robustness to missing channels.
5. **Complexity tradeoff:** naive all-channels-as-tokens inflates sequence length `C×N` and quadratic attention cost. The cross-attention-to-fixed-latent trick (Panopticon, Flex early fusion, Perceiver) collapses this back to `N×D` *before* the main transformer — this is how you avoid the blow-up in both embedding size *and* compute.

---

## Recommendation

For your stated case (same-size channel embeddings, arbitrary `C`, want a fixed-size joint embedding, no concatenation blow-up):

- **Default choice: attention pooling** — a learned query (or `k` queries) cross-attending over the channel-embedding set, with additive channel-identity embeddings and a channel-tied projection. This is exactly what ChannelViT / ChAda-ViT / Panopticon / Flex do, and it generalizes from 1 to dozens of channels.
- **If you have no per-channel metadata and want the simplest possible mechanism: Deep Sets** (`φ` per channel + sum/mean/max pool + `ρ`), as in IFANI. Cheap and order-invariant, but less expressive.
- **If channels carry physical metadata (wavelength, band) and you may see new channels at inference: hypernetwork conditioning** (DOFA/HyperFree) — the strongest flexibility, at the cost of needing that metadata.

A good practical compromise many of these converge on: **per-channel shared projection → add channel embedding → single-query cross-attention bottleneck**, trained with channel-subset sampling. It gives you one fixed `D`-vector per location for any channel count, retains channel identity, and keeps compute bounded.

Here's a survey of the established solution families, ordered from simplest to most expressive. Since you specifically have *same-size per-channel embeddings* and want a **fixed-size joint embedding** regardless of channel count, the relevant mechanisms all share one idea: **treat the channel axis as a set** and reduce it with a function that is agnostic to its cardinality.

---

## The core framing: channels as a set

If your per-channel embedding is `E_c ∈ R^D` (one vector per channel at a given spatial location/patch), you want `f({E_1..E_C}) → R^D` that works for any `C`. Any valid `f` should ideally be **permutation-invariant** w.r.t. channel order (so the model isn't order-sensitive) yet still **channel-aware** (so it can tell a red from a near-IR channel). Everything below is a variant of "encode each channel → aggregate the set → re-embed," with different aggregation and channel-identity schemes.

---

## Family A — Deep Sets / permutation-invariant pooling (sum, mean, max)

The classic recipe (Zaheer et al., "Deep Sets") is `f(S) = ρ( Σ_{c∈S} φ(E_c) )`. The aggregation is `sum / mean / max`, so the output dimension is fixed regardless of `C`.

Concrete image-domain uses:

- **IFANI** (General Image Fusion for an Arbitrary Number of Inputs, PMC9002723) applies a **shared conv to each input, then max-pooling across the N inputs** to get a single salient feature map, which is concatenated back to each branch. The permutation-invariance from the symmetric max-pool is exactly what lets it take an arbitrary, unordered number of inputs.
- **Deep Multi-Modal Sets** (ar5iv 2003.01607) formalizes modality/channel collections as sets to guarantee invariance to both permutation and cardinality.

**Pros:** trivial, cheap, dimension-stable, order-invariant. **Cons:** a plain mean/max treats all channels with equal (data-independent) weight — it can't learn that channel *c* matters more for *this* sample.

---

## Family B — Attention-based pooling over channels (the workhorse)

This is the most common modern answer to your exact problem: a **learnable query (or queries) cross-attends over the set of channel embeddings**, producing a fixed number of output vectors of size `D`.

**`joint = MHA(query=Q, key=K, value=V)` where K,V are the per-channel embeddings.** With one query token you collapse `(C, D) → (1, D)`; with `k` queries you get `(k, D)` (Pooling by Multihead Attention, "PMA," from Set Transformer — see SetONet arxiv 2505.04738, which reports attention pooling beats mean/sum especially under variable/drop-off configurations, ~5× lower error).

Concrete architectures:

- **ChannelViT** (arxiv 2309.16108) — patchifies **each channel separately** with a **channel-tied linear projection**, then adds a learnable **channel embedding `chn_c`** plus a **shared positional embedding**. Treating the channel dimension as the sequence dimension means the architecture "seamlessly handles inputs with varying sets of channels." Their ablation shows channel identity embeddings are critical (removing/mean-averaging them tanks performance). They also introduce **Hierarchical Channel Sampling (HCS)** for training robustness to unseen channel subsets.
- **ChAda-ViT** (arxiv 2311.15264) — designed explicitly for **arbitrary number, order, and type of channels** (1–10 microscopy channels). Uses an **Inter-Channel Attention** on top of spatial attention, with **channel embeddings + shared positional embeddings**, and a **padding-and-masking** scheme to standardize variable channel counts into a fixed sequence (NLP-style mask excludes pad tokens from attention).
- **Panopticon** (arxiv 2503.10845) — "**attention over channels as patch embedding**." Each channel goes through a shared 2D conv; the per-channel features become **keys/values for a cross-attention with a learned query**, reducing arbitrary `{c_i}` to a fixed `P² × D`. Spectral identity is injected via **wavelength positional encodings** on the keys/values.
- **Flex** (Emerging Flexible Designs for Geospatial MMFMs, alphaxiv 2606.12595) — tokenizes each channel independently to `(C×L, D)`, then an **early-fusion cross-attention aggregates across the C channels per spatial token**, guided by learnable channel embeddings, "reducing the sequence back to `(L, D)`… can accommodate any number of channels by simply adding or removing learnable embeddings."
- **Perceiver / Perceiver IO** (arxiv 2103.03206, 2107.14795) — the general version of this pattern: a cross-attention **latent bottleneck** maps an arbitrary input array to a fixed latent set, decoupling computation from input cardinality (pad inputs with modality-specific embeddings).
- **AnySat** (arxiv 2412.14123) / **OmniSat** — a **modality-combiner** that runs self-attention over modality tokens then a **cross-attention block** with a shared learned value token to merge an arbitrary set of modalities/channels into one embedding per patch.

**Why this is the right default:** the joint embedding stays `D`-dimensional no matter how many channels you feed, aggregation weights are **data-dependent** (unlike mean pooling), and channel identity is preserved through additive **channel embeddings** (learnable ID or metadata-derived).

Sketch:

```python
# per-channel embeddings: E [B, C, D], channel_ids: [B, C]
E = E + channel_embed(channel_ids)          # channel identity (learnable or wavelength PE)
K = V = E
Q = learned_queries.expand(B, k, D)         # k=1 for single joint embedding
joint = CrossAttention(Q, K, V, mask)       # [B, k, D]  -> fixed size, any C
# optionally add channel-tied per-channel projection before this
```

---

## Family C — Hypernetwork / dynamic-weight conditioning

Instead of aggregating channel tokens, these **generate the embedding weights from channel metadata**, so channel count never enters the embedding dimension at all.

- **DOFA** (arxiv 2403.15356) — a **wavelength-conditioned dynamic hypernetwork**: it positional-encodes each band's central wavelength and generates the patch-embedding conv weights on the fly. "The patch embedding layer achieves independence from the number of spectral bands." Works for **any number of input channels**, including unseen sensors (via weight-space interpolation). Code: github.com/zhu-xlab/DOFA.
- **HyperFree / HyperVision** (arxiv 2605.17286) — "**wavelengths as lookup keys**": a learned weight dictionary over the spectrum is assembled per-input, turning arbitrary channel configs into a **unified, fixed-length token sequence**. No structural change or retraining when channels change.

**Pros:** elegant, physically grounded, zero-padding-free, generalizes to new bands. **Cons:** needs meaningful channel metadata (wavelength etc.), and you must treat metadata-less channels specially (DOFA assigns default RGB wavelengths).

---

## Practical design decisions (apply across families)

1. **Channel identity is non-negotiable.** All sources (ChannelViT ablation, ChAda-ViT, Panopticon, AnySat) inject channel identity via additive embeddings — **learnable IDs** for fixed known channels, or **metadata-derived positional encodings** (wavelength/mode) for open-ended channels. Averaging them away destroys performance.
2. **Tie the per-channel projection across channels.** ChannelViT finds **shared/tied linear filters outperform untied** ones — low-level filters transfer across channels, and tying improves robustness to varying channel sets.
3. **Handle variable counts two ways:** (a) **pad + mask** into a fixed max length (ChAda-ViT, Panopticon), or (b) use **count-agnostic pooling** (attention/Deep Sets) so no padding is needed. Attention pooling is preferable when channel sets vary a lot.
4. **Regularize for partial/unseen channel subsets during training** — HCS (ChannelViT) samples the *number* of channels uniformly then a combination, giving an unbiased distribution over `m`; this dramatically improves test-time robustness to missing channels.
5. **Complexity tradeoff:** naive all-channels-as-tokens inflates sequence length `C×N` and quadratic attention cost. The cross-attention-to-fixed-latent trick (Panopticon, Flex early fusion, Perceiver) collapses this back to `N×D` *before* the main transformer — this is how you avoid the blow-up in both embedding size *and* compute.

---

## Recommendation

For your stated case (same-size channel embeddings, arbitrary `C`, want a fixed-size joint embedding, no concatenation blow-up):

- **Default choice: attention pooling** — a learned query (or `k` queries) cross-attending over the channel-embedding set, with additive channel-identity embeddings and a channel-tied projection. This is exactly what ChannelViT / ChAda-ViT / Panopticon / Flex do, and it generalizes from 1 to dozens of channels.
- **If you have no per-channel metadata and want the simplest possible mechanism: Deep Sets** (`φ` per channel + sum/mean/max pool + `ρ`), as in IFANI. Cheap and order-invariant, but less expressive.
- **If channels carry physical metadata (wavelength, band) and you may see new channels at inference: hypernetwork conditioning** (DOFA/HyperFree) — the strongest flexibility, at the cost of needing that metadata.

A good practical compromise many of these converge on: **per-channel shared projection → add channel embedding → single-query cross-attention bottleneck**, trained with channel-subset sampling. It gives you one fixed `D`-vector per location for any channel count, retains channel identity, and keeps compute bounded.

For a **high-content imaging (HCI) foundation model** — cellular fluorescence microscopy with panels like DNA/Hoechst, actin, tubulin, mitochondria, Golgi, plus increasingly multiplexed marker panels (CyCIF, CODEX, IMC at 20–60 channels) — the right choice is **Family B: attention pooling over channel embeddings**, and specifically a **ChAda-ViT / ChannelViT-style design**, *not* the wavelength-hypernetwork family (C).

## Why Family B wins for HCI specifically

**The decisive property: HCI channels are semantically non-interchangeable.** Unlike satellite bands, where a channel's identity is physically encoded by its wavelength, in HCI the same emission wavelength can carry completely different biology depending on the dye/marker attached. A nuclear (DNA) channel, a membrane channel, and a mitochondrial channel are functionally distinct token types. Consequences:

- **Pure Deep Sets (Family A) is a poor fit.** Mean/max pooling is permutation-invariant and therefore treats channels as an unordered bag — but the model *must* know that this token is "nucleus" and that one is "actin." You can patch this with channel embeddings, but a symmetric equal-weight pool still can't learn the strong data-dependent routing needed to compare, e.g., nuclear-vs-cytoplasmic spatial relationships. Deep Sets is a reasonable ablation baseline, not the architecture.
- **The metadata hypernetwork family (Family C) is a poor fit.** DOFA/HyperFree assume the channel's semantics are recoverable from a **wavelength / spectral lookup key**. In HCI, wavelength does not determine biology — a 488 nm channel is "actin" in one panel and "GFP-tagged protein" or "marker X" in another. Conditioning weights on wavelength would actively mislead the model. (You *could* substitute a learned *marker* lookup key for wavelength, which collapses Family C back toward a channel-embedding scheme anyway.)

**Why attention pooling is exactly right:** it gives you (i) a fixed-size joint embedding independent of channel count, (ii) **data-dependent** weighting across channels (so it can upweight the informative markers per sample), and (iii) explicit **channel-identity injection** so it remains aware of which marker each token is — which is the single most important factor in the ChAda-ViT and ChannelViT ablations.

## The concrete architecture to build

1. **Per-channel patch embedding, channel-tied:** patchify each channel independently through a **shared/tied** linear projection (ChannelViT shows tied filters beat untied and improve robustness to varying channel sets).
2. **Additive channel-identity embeddings** (critical — removing them destroys performance):
   - **Learnable per-marker embeddings** when the panel is closed/fixed.
   - For open, heterogeneous panels, prefer **semantic/text-conditioned channel embeddings** — e.g., the PhenoPLIFT approach, where each channel's identity comes from a **language prompt** ("DAPI nuclear stain", "phalloidin actin") encoded by a text encoder. This is the HCI-native answer to "what do I do for channels I've never seen," and generalizes `C` gracefully.
   - Keep a **shared spatial positional embedding** so position and channel identity don't conflate.
3. **Inter-channel attention / channel-as-sequence-dimension:** treat the channel axis as the sequence dimension. ChAda-ViT (channel-adaptive ViT, built explicitly for microscopy with arbitrary number/order/type of channels, validated on 1–10 channels) uses **inter-channel attention + padding-and-masking**; ChannelViT uses self-attention over concatenated channel tokens. Both reduce arbitrary `C` to a fixed joint representation.
4. **Collapse with a fixed query** (PMA / cross-attention bottleneck) to keep the joint embedding at fixed `D` and keep *compute* from blowing up — this is the Panopticon/Flex "attention over channels as patch embedding" pattern. For microscope images with many channels and large fields, doing this **before** the main spatial transformer matters.
5. **Train for missing channels / partial panels:** use **Hierarchical Channel Sampling** (ChannelViT) — sample the number of channels first, then a combination — which gives an unbiased distribution over channel subsets. HCI datasets are notorious for missing or variable panels (a "marker panel A" vs "panel B" split), so this is essential for cross-dataset transfer, not optional.
6. **Channel dropout / masking** as augmentation to handle the very common case of dropped channels across labs and instruments.

## Bottom line

- **Use:** channel-tied per-channel embedding → additive **channel-identity (or text-conditioned) embeddings** → **inter-channel cross-attention pooling to a fixed-size joint token**, trained with channel-subset sampling — i.e., the ChAda-ViT / ChannelViT family, with the PhenoPLIFT-style text prompt handling open/unseen markers.

For a **high-content imaging (HCI) foundation model** — cellular fluorescence microscopy with panels like DNA/Hoechst, actin, tubulin, mitochondria, Golgi, plus increasingly multiplexed marker panels (CyCIF, CODEX, IMC at 20–60 channels) — the right choice is **Family B: attention pooling over channel embeddings**, and specifically a **ChAda-ViT / ChannelViT-style design**, *not* the wavelength-hypernetwork family (C).

## Why Family B wins for HCI specifically

**The decisive property: HCI channels are semantically non-interchangeable.** Unlike satellite bands, where a channel's identity is physically encoded by its wavelength, in HCI the same emission wavelength can carry completely different biology depending on the dye/marker attached. A nuclear (DNA) channel, a membrane channel, and a mitochondrial channel are functionally distinct token types. Consequences:

- **Pure Deep Sets (Family A) is a poor fit.** Mean/max pooling is permutation-invariant and therefore treats channels as an unordered bag — but the model *must* know that this token is "nucleus" and that one is "actin." You can patch this with channel embeddings, but a symmetric equal-weight pool still can't learn the strong data-dependent routing needed to compare, e.g., nuclear-vs-cytoplasmic spatial relationships. Deep Sets is a reasonable ablation baseline, not the architecture.
- **The metadata hypernetwork family (Family C) is a poor fit.** DOFA/HyperFree assume the channel's semantics are recoverable from a **wavelength / spectral lookup key**. In HCI, wavelength does not determine biology — a 488 nm channel is "actin" in one panel and "GFP-tagged protein" or "marker X" in another. Conditioning weights on wavelength would actively mislead the model. (You *could* substitute a learned *marker* lookup key for wavelength, which collapses Family C back toward a channel-embedding scheme anyway.)

**Why attention pooling is exactly right:** it gives you (i) a fixed-size joint embedding independent of channel count, (ii) **data-dependent** weighting across channels (so it can upweight the informative markers per sample), and (iii) explicit **channel-identity injection** so it remains aware of which marker each token is — which is the single most important factor in the ChAda-ViT and ChannelViT ablations.

## The concrete architecture to build

1. **Per-channel patch embedding, channel-tied:** patchify each channel independently through a **shared/tied** linear projection (ChannelViT shows tied filters beat untied and improve robustness to varying channel sets).
2. **Additive channel-identity embeddings** (critical — removing them destroys performance):
   - **Learnable per-marker embeddings** when the panel is closed/fixed.
   - For open, heterogeneous panels, prefer **semantic/text-conditioned channel embeddings** — e.g., the PhenoPLIFT approach, where each channel's identity comes from a **language prompt** ("DAPI nuclear stain", "phalloidin actin") encoded by a text encoder. This is the HCI-native answer to "what do I do for channels I've never seen," and generalizes `C` gracefully.
   - Keep a **shared spatial positional embedding** so position and channel identity don't conflate.
3. **Inter-channel attention / channel-as-sequence-dimension:** treat the channel axis as the sequence dimension. ChAda-ViT (channel-adaptive ViT, built explicitly for microscopy with arbitrary number/order/type of channels, validated on 1–10 channels) uses **inter-channel attention + padding-and-masking**; ChannelViT uses self-attention over concatenated channel tokens. Both reduce arbitrary `C` to a fixed joint representation.
4. **Collapse with a fixed query** (PMA / cross-attention bottleneck) to keep the joint embedding at fixed `D` and keep *compute* from blowing up — this is the Panopticon/Flex "attention over channels as patch embedding" pattern. For microscope images with many channels and large fields, doing this **before** the main spatial transformer matters.
5. **Train for missing channels / partial panels:** use **Hierarchical Channel Sampling** (ChannelViT) — sample the number of channels first, then a combination — which gives an unbiased distribution over channel subsets. HCI datasets are notorious for missing or variable panels (a "marker panel A" vs "panel B" split), so this is essential for cross-dataset transfer, not optional.
6. **Channel dropout / masking** as augmentation to handle the very common case of dropped channels across labs and instruments.

- **Use:** channel-tied per-channel embedding → additive **channel-identity (or text-conditioned) embeddings** → **inter-channel cross-attention pooling to a fixed-size joint token**, trained with channel-subset sampling — i.e., the ChAda-ViT / ChannelViT family, with the PhenoPLIFT-style text prompt handling open/unseen markers.

116f1fc7-ae71-49f7-9745-596befe030b0.content:
Yes — and the key realization is that **padding was never intrinsic to the design; it was an artifact of representing the channel set as a dense `[B, C_max, D]` tensor.** All the HCI-relevant properties (arbitrary `C`, channel-identity awareness, data-dependent weighting, cross-panel generalization) live in the *operators*, not the tensor shape. If you make every operator cardinality-agnostic, you delete padding entirely.

## Why padding is avoidable in principle

Attention pooling, Deep Sets pooling, and Perceiver-style cross-attention are all **set functions** — they accept a variable number of vectors and return a fixed-size output. None of them *needs* a pad token. The only reason ChAda-ViT uses padding-and-masking is to batch heterogeneous samples onto a dense GPU grid. Remove that requirement (or satisfy it with varlen kernels) and padding disappears.

## The three practical routes

### 1. Varlen (unpadded) attention — the standard "padding-free transformer"
Flatten all channels from all samples in a batch into a single `[ΣC, D]` sequence and pass **cumulative sequence-length offsets** instead of an attention mask. This is exactly HuggingFace's padding-free path and FlashAttention's `varlen` API (`cu_seqlens`).

```python
# channels of all samples concatenated; no pad tokens ever created
E    = per_channel_proj(tokens) + channel_embed(ids)   # [ΣC, D]
joint = varlen_cross_attn(q=queries, k=E, v=E,
                          cu_seqlens=offsets)          # [B, k, D]
```
- Attention mathematically already ignores other samples; varlen just exploits that.
- You keep **per-token** LayerNorm (never normalize across the channel axis), so variable `C` never biases statistics.
- Channel identity rides along as an **additive marker/channel embedding** on each real token — no placeholder pad row in the embedding table.

### 2. Nested / jagged tensors
PyTorch **nested tensors** (and TF **RaggedTensor**) natively hold variable-length dims; ops dispatch to fused kernels. Cleanest code, at the cost of some kernel coverage — best when your `C` varies a lot across samples.

### 3. Cardinality-agnostic pooling that never needed a mask anyway
- **PMA / fixed-query cross-attention** with variable-length K/V: output size is set by the *number of learned queries*, independent of `C`. Inherently padding-free.
- **Weighted-sum-by-hypernetwork:** produce a per-channel weight `w_c = MLP(channel_embed_c)` and compute `joint = Σ_c softmax(w)_c · E_c`. This is a gated Deep Sets pool — `O(C)` instead of `O(C²)`, no attention matrix, no padding. Attractive for **20–60 channel multiplexed panels** where quadratic channel attention cost is the concern.

## Directly relevant HCI considerations

1. **Handle missing channels by omission, not zero-padding.** This is the big win. With a cardinality-agnostic pool, a dropped channel is simply *absent from the set* — it never enters attention. Zero-padding + masking leaks unless perfectly masked and still skews normalization; omission is exact and cheaper. This is the correct default for cross-lab/cross-panel data, and it composes cleanly with **Hierarchical Channel Sampling** (sample channel *count* first, then combination) for training robustness.

2. **Channel identity without a pad vocabulary.** Since HCI semantics aren't wavelength-determined, use:
   - **Learnable per-marker embeddings** for closed panels, or
   - **Text-prompt-conditioned embeddings** (PhenoPLIFT-style) so unseen markers still get a meaningful identity vector — no fixed-size lookup table, hence no pad slot, and `C` is truly unbounded.
   
   Because identity is additive and per-token, adding/removing a channel just adds/removes its embedding.

3. **Permutation behavior is preserved.** Attention is permutation-equivariant in the K/V set; adding channel-identity embeddings makes the output depend on *which* marker is present, not on *order* — exactly what you want for unordered panels. (If you ever want strict order-invariance over a channel *group*, slot-pool within groups.)

4. **Batching efficiency.** The only real cost of padding-free is uneven `C` across a batch. Mitigations: (a) sort/bucket samples by `C` so varlen segments are similar length, or (b) for fixed-panel datasets just run dense unbatched-by-C — either way you're not paying for pad tokens.

5. **Dropout/augmentation stay clean.** Implement channel dropout by **removing tokens before the channel-attention stack**, not by zeroing channels — the pool then behaves identically at train and test.

## Bottom line

Padding-free is not a compromise — for HCI it's *better*: **varlen cross-attention into a fixed query bottleneck (or a hypernetwork-weighted sum), with additive marker/text-conditioned channel embeddings, per-token norm, and channel-set sampling.** You keep every property that matters — arbitrary/unbounded `C`, explicit channel identity, data-dependent weighting, and exact handling of missing channels — while eliminating pad tokens, mask bookkeeping, and the statistical skew that padding introduces. The ChAda-ViT-style pad-and-mask is purely a densification convenience; swap it for `cu_seqlens`/nested tensors and the architecture becomes genuinely set-native.

## The honest gap

The property you want — **unbounded `C`, fixed embedding, no pad tokens, no concat blow-up** — is satisfied *architecturally* by CellRep, OpenPhenom, and DOFA, but the shipped code (where available) still typically densifies to `[B, C_max, …]` for batching. ChAda-ViT, the most cited HCI model, is explicitly the padded/masked design. So there is no drop-in "HCI + varlen channel attention" repo yet — you'd be building the first, but on solid foundations.

## Recommended build paths (ranked)

**1. Fork CellRep as your backbone (best fit for your stated constraints).**
It already gives you a **fixed-size joint embedding** from arbitrary `C` via channel-axis mean pooling, plus channel-identity embeddings and channel-order permutation augmentation. To make it genuinely padding-free, replace the dense channel stack with varlen/nested tensors and keep the pool. This is the least code to reach your goal, and `cellrepDINO` weights are public.

**2. Fork ChannelViT and extend its HCS token-exclusion path to inference.**
Its HCS logic *already* omits tokens instead of masking — you just need to generalize that beyond training and swap the backbone's fixed `in_chans` stack for packed sequences. You also inherit the strongest robustness recipe (two-stage channel-subset sampling) for free.

**3. Use OpenPhenom's channelwise cross-attention as the fusion module, rebuilt varlen.**
Its fixed-query cross-attention over per-channel tokens is exactly the "collapse `C` → 1 token of size `D`" operator you want; wrap it in the varlen primitives below. Caveat: non-commercial license and unverified internal padding.

**4. If you may see unseen markers, borrow DOFA's hypernetwork idea but key it on marker identity, not wavelength.**

## The low-level plumbing to make any of these varlen

All of these are one change away from padding-free once the fusion is a set function:

- **`torch.nn.attention.varlen_attn`** (PyTorch's FlashAttention varlen API) with `cu_seq_q`/`cu_seq_k` — pack all channels of all samples into one `[ΣC, D]` sequence, no pad tokens. Official tutorial + docs exist.
- **Nested tensors** (`torch.jagged`) + `scaled_dot_product_attention` — PyTorch's own docs report ~**5.6× speedup and ~3.4 GB less peak memory** versus dense padding+mask, and it "eliminates the bug-prone practices of explicit padding and masking."
- **HuggingFace padding-free path** / `flash_attn_varlen_func` if you integrate with `transformers` backbones.
- Keep **per-token LayerNorm** (never normalize across the channel axis) so variable `C` doesn't skew statistics.

## Bottom line

Build on **CellRep** (fixed-embed, channel-invariant, public weights) or **ChannelViT** (already token-excludes under HCS, strongest missing-channel training recipe), and swap their dense channel stack for **`varlen_attn`/nested tensors**. ChAda-ViT and Panopticon are excellent architectural references but are explicitly padded-and-masked, so use them for the *attention design*, not the *batching strategy*. Do **not** start from uniDINO or PhenoSeq if fixed-size is a hard requirement — they concatenate and grow with `C`.

| Model | Channel mechanism | Padding status | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ChAda-ViT** (CVPR'24) | Inter-channel attention, per-channel patchify, channel embeddings | **Explicit padding + masking** — paper defines `C_max`, appends `pad_d` tokens, uses `src_key_padding_mask`. The canonical HCI reference, but the *opposite* of padding-free. | `github.com/nicoboou/chadvit` (Apache-2.0) |
| **ChannelViT** (insitro) | Learnable channel embeddings + Hierarchical Channel Sampling | **Closest to padding-free already.** Its HCS variant *excludes* unselected channel patches from the sequence ("we can simply exclude the patches… we don't need to reset pixels") rather than zero-filling. Its `multi_vit.py` runs a per-channel ViT then mean/max-aggregates — inherently variable-`C`. | `github.com/insitro/ChannelViT` |
| **OpenPhenom-S/16** (Recursion, CA-MAE) | Per-channel patch tokens → **channelwise cross-attention** → fixed 384-d | **Cardinality-agnostic by design**; model card explicitly tests `C ∈ {1,4,6,11}` and "any channel count or ordering." Cross-attention to a fixed representation means output size never depends on `C`. Internal densification not documented, so verify. | `huggingface.co/recursionpharma/OpenPhenom` (non-commercial) |
| **CellRep** (CVPRW'25) | Content-aware patch embed + channel-mixing transformer + **mean-pool over the `C` axis** → sequence length `L` | **Padding-free by construction** — pooling divides by `C`, so no `C_max` and no pad tokens. Also permutes channel order as augmentation. Truly fixed-size regardless of `C`. | `huggingface.co/lhphillips/cellrepDINO` (weights); CVPRW paper |
| **uniDINO** (Bayer) | Single-channel DINO features **concatenated** across channels | Padding-free (loads single channels), but **embedding grows linearly with `C`** — the exact thing you said you don't want. Useful as a baseline only. | `github.com/Bayer-Group/uniDINO` (BSD-3) |
| **Panopticon** (remote sensing) | Cross-attention over channel tokens with one learned query | **Explicitly "padding and masking"** for batch-inconsistent `C`. Great architecture template, not HCI data. | arXiv 2503.10845 |
| **DOFA** (remote sensing) | Wavelength-conditioned **hypernetwork** generates patch-embed weights | **Padding-free by construction** (weight count independent of `C`). Only reuse if you swap wavelength key → marker key. | `github.com/zhu-xlab/DOFA` |
| **CytoBERT** (not imaging) | Variable-panel transformer, attention pooling over marker tokens | **Set-native / padding-free** philosophy (variable panels), but cytometry not microscopy. Good conceptual reference for attention pooling. | `github.com/bckrlab/cytobert` |

The property you want — **unbounded `C`, fixed embedding, no pad tokens, no concat blow-up** — is satisfied *architecturally* by CellRep, OpenPhenom, and DOFA, but the shipped code (where available) still typically densifies to `[B, C_max, …]` for batching. ## Recommended build paths (ranked)

**1. Fork CellRep as your backbone (best fit for your stated constraints).**
It already gives you a **fixed-size joint embedding** from arbitrary `C` via channel-axis mean pooling, plus channel-identity embeddings and channel-order permutation augmentation. To make it genuinely padding-free, replace the dense channel stack with varlen/nested tensors and keep the pool. This is the least code to reach your goal, and `cellrepDINO` weights are public.

**2. Fork ChannelViT and extend its HCS token-exclusion path to inference.**
Its HCS logic *already* omits tokens instead of masking — you just need to generalize that beyond training and swap the backbone's fixed `in_chans` stack for packed sequences. You also inherit the strongest robustness recipe (two-stage channel-subset sampling) for free.

**3. Use OpenPhenom's channelwise cross-attention as the fusion module, rebuilt varlen.**
Its fixed-query cross-attention over per-channel tokens is exactly the "collapse `C` → 1 token of size `D`" operator you want; wrap it in the varlen primitives below. Caveat: non-commercial license and unverified internal padding.

**4. If you may see unseen markers, borrow DOFA's hypernetwork idea but key it on marker identity, not wavelength.**

## The low-level plumbing to make any of these varlen

All of these are one change away from padding-free once the fusion is a set function:

- **`torch.nn.attention.varlen_attn`** (PyTorch's FlashAttention varlen API) with `cu_seq_q`/`cu_seq_k` — pack all channels of all samples into one `[ΣC, D]` sequence, no pad tokens. Official tutorial + docs exist.
- **Nested tensors** (`torch.jagged`) + `scaled_dot_product_attention` — PyTorch's own docs report ~**5.6× speedup and ~3.4 GB less peak memory** versus dense padding+mask, and it "eliminates the bug-prone practices of explicit padding and masking."
- **HuggingFace padding-free path** / `flash_attn_varlen_func` if you integrate with `transformers` backbones.
- Keep **per-token LayerNorm** (never normalize across the channel axis) so variable `C` doesn't skew statistics.

## Bottom line

Build on **CellRep** (fixed-embed, channel-invariant, public weights) or **ChannelViT** (already token-excludes under HCS, strongest missing-channel training recipe), and swap their dense channel stack for **`varlen_attn`/nested tensors**. ChAda-ViT and Panopticon are excellent architectural references but are explicitly padded-and-masked, so use them for the *attention design*, not the *batching strategy*. Do **not** start from uniDINO or PhenoSeq if fixed-size is a hard requirement — they concatenate and grow with `C`.

# Handoff: Padding-Free Channel-Fusion Module for an HCI Foundation Model

**To:** Implementation agent
**From:** Research/design
**Deliverable:** A channel-fusion module (encoder front-end) that maps an **arbitrary, unordered set of same-size per-channel embeddings** to a **fixed-size joint embedding**, with **no padding tokens**, tuned for high-content imaging (HCI) foundation models.

---

## 1. Problem statement

Input: a set of per-channel embeddings `{E_c ∈ R^D}` for c ∈ panel, where `C` varies per sample (1 channel up to 20–60+ for multiplexed panels), channel order is semantically meaningless, and panels/markers vary across labs and datasets.

We need `f({E_c}) → R^{k×D}` (k learned queries, typically k=1) such that:
- Output size is **independent of C** (no concatenation blow-up).
- `C` is **unbounded** (unseen markers, new panels).
- Output is **permutation-invariant** over channel order but **channel-identity-aware**.
- Aggregation weights are **data-dependent** (not fixed mean/max).
- **Missing channels handled by omission**, not zero-padding.
- No pad tokens, no attention masks for cardinality.

---

## 2. Design decisions (already settled — implement these)

**Chosen family: attention pooling over channel embeddings** (ChannelViT / ChAda-ViT / Panopticon pattern), made set-native. Explicitly **rejected**:
- Deep Sets mean/max as *primary* mechanism (channels are not interchangeable — identity required).
- Wavelength-hypernetwork conditioning (DOFA/HyperFree) — **semantically invalid for HCI**: emission wavelength does not determine biology. Only reuse the hypernetwork idea if the lookup key is **marker identity**, not wavelength.

**Pipeline (in order):**

1. **Per-channel patch embedding, channel-tied.** Shared/tied linear projection across channels (ChannelViT shows tied > untied; better robustness to varying channel sets).
2. **Additive channel-identity embedding** per token — **critical, do not omit** (removing it destroys performance in both ChannelViT and ChAda-ViT ablations).
   - Closed/fixed panel → learnable per-marker embeddings.
   - Open/multiplexed panels → **text-prompt-conditioned channel embeddings** (PhenoPLIFT-style: encode a prompt like `"DAPI nuclear stain"`, `"phalloidin actin"` with a text encoder, use as the identity vector). This is what makes `C` truly unbounded with no fixed lookup table and hence **no pad slot**.
   - Add a **shared spatial positional embedding** so position ≠ channel identity.
3. **Channel-axis attention / pooling** to a fixed query bottleneck (PMA-style cross-attention). Put this **before** the main spatial transformer to bound compute.
4. **Per-token LayerNorm** everywhere — **never normalize across the channel axis** (variable `C` would bias statistics).

---

## 3. Padding-free implementation (the core requirement)

Do **not** densify to `[B, C_max, D]`. Instead:

**Primary route — varlen attention (`cu_seqlens`):**
```python
# Concatenate only REAL channel tokens across the whole batch — no pad tokens ever created.
E    = per_channel_proj(tokens) + channel_embed(ids)      # [ΣC, D], ids carry marker identity
joint = varlen_cross_attn(q=queries,                      # [B, k, D]
                          k=E, v=E,
                          cu_seqlens=offsets)              # cumulative channel counts per sample
```
- Attention is already cross-sample-independent; varlen just exploits it, so results match masked attention exactly.
- **Implement channel dropout / augmentation by REMOVING tokens before the channel-attention stack**, never by zeroing.

**Alternates (choose by kernel coverage / variance of C):**
- **PyTorch nested tensors** (or TF RaggedTensor) — cleanest when `C` varies a lot; use if fused kernels cover all ops.
- **Hypernetwork-weighted sum** (pad-free, `O(C)` instead of `O(C²)`): `w_c = MLP(channel_embed_c)`, `joint = Σ_c softmax(w)_c · E_c`. Preferred if 20–60-channel quadratic channel-attention cost is a concern. Validate against the cross-attention route.

**Batching efficiency:** sort/bucket samples by `C` so varlen segments are similar length. Memory is a non-issue (no pad waste), but uneven segments may underutilize kernels.

---

## 4. HCI-specific requirements (must-have)

1. **Missing channels by omission.** Cross-lab/cross-panel data is the norm; a dropped channel must simply be absent from the set. Verify exact-equivalence (§5).
2. **Hierarchical Channel Sampling (HCS)** during training: sample channel *count* first, then a combination — gives an unbiased distribution over channel subsets and is **essential** for cross-dataset transfer and robustness to partial panels.
3. **Channel-subset regularization**: train on random marker subsets, not just full panels.
4. **Open-vocabulary identity**: implement the text-conditioned embedding path so unseen markers get a meaningful identity vector without resizing any table.
5. **Permutation semantics**: attention is permutation-equivariant over K/V; with additive identity embeddings the output depends on *which* markers are present, not order. If any downstream step needs strict order-invariance over a channel *group*, slot-pool within groups.

---

## 5. Acceptance criteria / tests

- [ ] **Cardinality invariance:** output tensor shape identical for `C ∈ {1, 3, 6, 20, 60}`.
- [ ] **Padding-free equivalence:** padding-free module output ≡ masked-padded reference within numerical tolerance, across mixed-`C` batches.
- [ ] **Omission correctness:** removing a channel == feeding that channel with attention fully excluded (verify no leakage; check that per-token norm is unaffected).
- [ ] **Permutation test:** shuffling channel order changes output < tolerance (identity-dependent, order-independent).
- [ ] **Identity ablation:** dropping the additive channel embedding degrades a benchmark task (reproduce the ChannelViT ablation) — confirms the embedding is wired in correctly.
- [ ] **Open-vocabulary test:** an unseen marker's text prompt yields a usable embedding; no table resizing, no pad slot.
- [ ] **No pad artifacts:** assert no `-inf` masks and no `[B, C_max, D]` tensors in the fusion path unless that axis is genuinely dense.
- [ ] **Cost check:** report FLOPs/throughput for C=60 comparing cross-attention vs. hypernetwork-weighted-sum.

---

## 6. Pitfalls to avoid

- **Do not** fall back to `[B, C_max, D]` + masking "for convenience" — that reintroduces the statistical skew and pad bookkeeping this task exists to remove.
- **Do not** use mean/max pooling as the primary mechanism; symmetric equal-weight pooling cannot learn the data-dependent routing HCI needs.
- **Do not** condition on wavelength — it's the wrong key for HCI (use marker/text identity).
- **Do not** normalize across the channel axis at any point.
- **Do not** implement channel dropout by zeroing.

---

## 7. Reference implementations to adapt

- **ChannelViT** (arXiv 2309.16108) — channel-as-sequence, tied projection, identity embeddings, HCS.
- **ChAda-ViT** (arXiv 2311.15264) — arbitrary channel count/order/type; replace its pad-and-mask with varlen.
- **Panopticon** (arXiv 2503.10845) — attention-over-channels-as-patch-embedding with a fixed learned query.
- **Perceiver / Perceiver IO** (arXiv 2103.03206 / 2107.14795) — general fixed-latent cross-attention bottleneck.
- **PhenoPLIFT** (text-prompt channel conditioning for microscopy) — for the open-vocabulary identity path.
- FlashAttention `varlen` API (`cu_seqlens`) / HF padding-free path; PyTorch nested tensors.

---

## 8. Deliverable summary

Ship `ChannelFusion` as a drop-in encoder front-end: **channel-tied per-channel embedding → additive marker/text-conditioned identity embedding → varlen cross-attention into a fixed learned-query bottleneck**, trained with HCS + channel dropout **by token removal**, per-token norms throughout. Padding-free is not a compromise here — it is the correct default for HCI, giving exact missing-channel handling and unbounded `C` while keeping channel identity and data-dependent weighting.

2. **Hierarchical Channel Sampling (HCS)** during training: sample channel *count* first, then a combination — gives an unbiased distribution over channel subsets and is **essential** for cross-dataset transfer and robustness to partial panels.
3. **Channel-subset regularization**: train on random marker subsets, not just full panels.
4. **Open-vocabulary identity**: implement the text-conditioned embedding path so unseen markers get a meaningful identity vector without resizing any table.

- [ ] **Permutation test:** shuffling channel order changes output < tolerance (identity-dependent, order-independent).
- [ ] **Identity ablation:** dropping the additive channel embedding degrades a benchmark task (reproduce the ChannelViT ablation) — confirms the embedding is wired in correctly.

- **Do not** normalize across the channel axis at any point.

# Yes — and it's arguably the *right* pretraining objective for this backbone

Continuing the handoff: a masked-autoencoder (MAE) objective is not merely compatible with the padding-free channel-fusion design; it's a better fit than it is for a standard ViT, and the HCI literature has converged on it independently. But there is **one mandatory adaptation** (channel masking) and **one architectural tension** (the fusion bottleneck) you must resolve.

---

## 1. Why padding-free and MAE are a perfect match

Standard MAE is already a **set-drop** operation: the encoder sees only visible patch tokens, mask tokens appear only in the decoder. Your padding-free module **drops tokens by construction** (`cu_seqlens`), so:

- Spatial masking = simply omit those rows from the `E [ΣC_visible, D]` tensor before channel fusion. No mask tokens, no `-inf` attention mask.
- Channel masking = omit entire channels from the set. This is *exactly* the "missing channel by omission" property you already designed for — it becomes the training signal instead of an inference edge case.

This is strictly cleaner than the ChAda-ViT pad-and-mask route, where masked/pad tokens must be threaded through attention and risk leaking. Your design makes masking **lossless by construction**.

---

## 2. The mandatory adaptation: mask the channel axis too (this is the HCI-specific finding)

Do **not** rely on spatial patch masking alone. The key empirical result from **ChA-MAEViT (arXiv 2503.19331)**:

> Standard MAEs assume image channels are redundant (true for RGB), so patch masking is reconstructable from cross-channel correlation. **This assumption fails in multi-channel imaging (MCI)**, where channels are complementary with minimal overlap. Pure patch masking therefore only learns *intra-channel* structure and fails to exploit cross-channel interactions.

Their fix — **Dynamic Channel-Patch (DCP) masking** — combines:
1. **Random patch masking** with *independently sampled* locations per channel (not one mask replicated across channels).
2. **Dynamic channel masking**: sample the number of channels to mask `k ~ U{0,…,C-1}`, then sample *which* `k` — i.e. **HCS repurposed from a regularizer into a supervision target**. Masked channels' patches are not dropped from the loss; they become the reconstruction targets.
3. A mix probability `p_patch, p_channel` to choose patch-masking vs channel-masking per step.

This unifies the "channel-subset regularization" already in your spec with the pretraining objective: **you get the cross-panel robustness regularizer and the representation-learning signal from the same masking procedure.**

Their results on **CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, So2Sat**: +3.0–21.5% over SOTA MCI-ViTs, and it directly yields **robustness to varying channel configurations** at inference.

Corroborating evidence that channel masking is the point:
- **MIM-CyCIF** (Sims et al., *Commun. Biol.* 2024; PMLR v240) — channel-wise masking of 25 CyCIF markers, single-cell images reshaped so each "patch" is one channel; the MAE objective becomes **marker imputation / panel reduction** directly.
- **CA-MAE** (Recursion, CVPR 2024) — channel-agnostic MAE that generalizes across channel counts/orders, pretrained on RPI-93M, evaluated zero-shot-ish on JUMP-CP with a *different* channel structure. Code: `github.com/recursionpharma/maes_microscopy`.
- **ChannelMAE** (`github.com/saiprabhakar/ChannelMAE`) — a direct MAE + ChannelViT fusion; `models_chamae.py`.
- **SatMAE** group-channel variant — shows the same pattern works for grouped channels (`spatial_mask` toggle: mask a spatial location across all channels vs. independently per channel).
- **VirTues** (bio.rodeo) — full MAE where "fully masked channels can be inpainted," i.e. **virtual staining as a pretraining byproduct**.

---

## 3. The architectural tension you must resolve: fusion bottleneck vs. reconstruction fidelity

The single-query cross-attention collapses `C → k` vectors. For MAE you must reconstruct the *masked channels' raw pixels* from that joint embedding. If `k=1`, you're training a `C → 1 → C` autoencoder — the bottleneck may be too lossy to give a strong reconstruction gradient (kills the SSL signal), or too lossy to preserve per-channel detail.

Resolutions (in increasing order of preference):

1. **Increase `k`** (multi-query PMA). Modest, easy. But it dilutes the fixed-size-representation virtue if `k` grows with `C`.
2. **Add memory / register tokens** — this is **ChA-MAEViT's** explicit remedy: learnable tokens carried through *both* encoder and decoder "as long-term memory to retain key cross-channel information," addressing "structurally diverse channels" that can't be reconstructed from each other. Keep them fixed-count and independent of `C`.
3. **Keep channel tokens alive through the encoder** (not fully collapsed before the decoder). ChA-MAEViT argues against fully pre-collapsing; a **Channel-Aware Decoder**, shared across all channels (scales to 18+ channels; per-channel decoders do not), consumes per-channel tokens + memory tokens. Note this slightly weakens the "fuse before the spatial transformer" compute argument — a reasonable tradeoff is: **fuse for the *representation* path, but expose the unmasked channel tokens to the light decoder** for reconstruction.
4. **Factorized marker × spatial attention** — **VirTues** splits attention into a marker axis and a spatial axis rather than joint, explicitly "avoiding the quadratic blow-up that makes standard ViTs impractical on high-plex imaging." This is the cleanest way to keep both per-channel fidelity and bounded compute, and it composes with your varlen padding-free path on each axis.

Recommendation: **k=1 fixed query for the pretrained representation output, plus fixed-count memory tokens, plus a shared channel-aware decoder that can also see the unmasked channel tokens.** Validate against the multi-query variant.

---

## 4. Decoder must be conditioned on channel identity

When reconstructing a masked channel, the decoder must know **which** marker it's reconstructing. Your **additive channel-identity embedding** (learnable marker ID or text-conditioned) is not just for the encoder — feed the target channel's identity vector to the decoder as well. This turns the identity embedding into a **target specification** and is what lets one shared decoder handle all channels:

> ChA-MAEViT: "a shared lightweight decoder utilizes channel tokens to provide channel-specific behavior."

This also sets up open-vocabulary nicely (§6).

---

## 5. Loss

Per-channel **normalized pixel loss** over masked patches (standard MAE normalizes per patch; for MCI normalize **per channel** so heterogeneous intensity ranges don't bias the objective). ChA-MAEViT reports Spearman correlation of mean intensity + SSIM as the HCI-relevant reconstruction metrics.

---

## 6. Novel / unseen channels — now a strength

Because your identity embeddings can be **text-conditioned** (PhenoPLIFT-style), you get a route to zero-shot identity that ChA-MAEViT had to approximate: they initialize new channel tokens randomly and **fine-tune only the channel tokens (rest frozen) using the reconstruction loss on a few unlabeled test images** — improving novel-channel accuracy from 9.2% to 11.6% with 640 unlabeled images. Text-conditioned identity should beat random init *before* any fine-tuning, and VirTues demonstrates the stronger version: **sequence-grounded marker tokens (ESM-2 embeddings of the protein's UniProt sequence) fused with image content**, giving "zero-shot transfer across panels and platforms," including technologies never seen in pretraining.

If your channels carry a protein/marker name, wiring an ESM-2 embedding in as the identity vector is the single highest-leverage upgrade to your identity path.

---

## 7. What MAE buys you on this backbone (HCI downstream payoffs)

- **Virtual staining / marker imputation as a free byproduct** — masked-channel reconstruction *is* imputation (MIM-CyCIF, miniMTI, VirTues, "Language of Stains").
- **Panel reduction** — use reconstruction fidelity to rank marker subsets (iterative panel selection in MIM-CyCIF / miniMTI).
- **Cross-panel / cross-technology transfer** — CA-MAE and VirTues both demonstrate generalization to unseen channel structures.
- **Stronger than weakly-supervised** — Recursion's CA-MAE reports up to **+11.5% relative** improvement recalling curated biological relationships vs. weak supervision.

---

## 8. Deltas to add to the handoff spec

**Additions to §2 (design):**
- Two masking axes: **spatial patch masking** (independently sampled per channel) + **dynamic channel masking** (HCS-style: sample `k`, then the subset). Mix via `p_patch, p_channel`.
- **Fixed-count memory/register tokens** through encoder + decoder (cardinality-independent — does not break padding-free).
- **Channel-aware shared decoder** (one decoder, not per-channel), optionally fed the unmasked channel tokens + memory tokens.

**Additions to §3 (padding-free):**
- Masking = **token omission** in the varlen tensor (spatial mask drops patch rows; channel mask drops channel rows). No mask tokens, no attention masks for masking.
- Guard: never mask *all* channels (keep ≥1 visible) unless doing pure spatial-only steps.

**Additions to §4 (HCI requirements):**
- Identity embedding is reused **as decoder target conditioning**.
- Optionally replace learnable marker embeddings with **sequence-grounded (ESM-2) identity vectors** for zero-shot new-marker transfer.
- Explicit "novel-channel" protocol: freeze model, adapt only identity vectors via reconstruction loss on a few unlabeled images.

**Additions to §5 (acceptance criteria):**
- [ ] Channel-masked reconstruction: masked-channel output achieves target Spearman/SSIM on a held-out panel; visibly beats spatial-only masking ablation.
- [ ] DCP vs. patch-only ablation reproduced (expect a large gap on MCI, per ChA-MAEViT).
- [ ] Memory-token ablation: removing them degrades masked-channel reconstruction.
- [ ] Zero-shot novel-channel: text/sequence-conditioned identity gives usable reconstruction **without** fine-tuning; report the fine-tuned-tokens upper bound.
- [ ] Padding-free property preserved under masking: encoder input length == number of *visible* tokens; assert no mask/pad tokens exist anywhere.
- [ ] Downstream linprobe transfer to a different-panel dataset.

**Pitfalls (add to §6):**
- **Do not** use patch-only masking as the primary objective — the HCI evidence says cross-channel learning won't happen.
- **Do not** fully collapse channels before the decoder — reconstruction fidelity collapses with it (add memory tokens / expose channel tokens).
- **Do not** use per-channel decoders — doesn't scale past a handful of channels.

---

**Bottom line:** Yes. Train it as a **channel-aware MAE** — padding-free token-drop for spatial masking, HCS-style dynamic channel masking as an explicit reconstruction target, memory tokens + shared channel-aware decoder conditioned on channel identity. This is the design validated by ChA-MAEViT, CA-MAE, MIM-CyCIF, and VirTues, and it turns your missing-channel robustness, open-vocabulary identity, and virtual-staining/imputation capabilities into things the pretraining objective *produces* rather than things you bolt on.

# Yes — and it's arguably the *right* pretraining objective for this backbone

Continuing the handoff: a masked-autoencoder (MAE) objective is not merely compatible with the padding-free channel-fusion design; it's a better fit than it is for a standard ViT, and the HCI literature has converged on it independently. But there is **one mandatory adaptation** (channel masking) and **one architectural tension** (the fusion bottleneck) you must resolve.

---

## 1. Why padding-free and MAE are a perfect match

Standard MAE is already a **set-drop** operation: the encoder sees only visible patch tokens, mask tokens appear only in the decoder. Your padding-free module **drops tokens by construction** (`cu_seqlens`), so:

- Spatial masking = simply omit those rows from the `E [ΣC_visible, D]` tensor before channel fusion. No mask tokens, no `-inf` attention mask.
- Channel masking = omit entire channels from the set. This is *exactly* the "missing channel by omission" property you already designed for — it becomes the training signal instead of an inference edge case.

This is strictly cleaner than the ChAda-ViT pad-and-mask route, where masked/pad tokens must be threaded through attention and risk leaking. Your design makes masking **lossless by construction**.

---

## 2. The mandatory adaptation: mask the channel axis too (this is the HCI-specific finding)

Do **not** rely on spatial patch masking alone. The key empirical result from **ChA-MAEViT (arXiv 2503.19331)**:

> Standard MAEs assume image channels are redundant (true for RGB), so patch masking is reconstructable from cross-channel correlation. **This assumption fails in multi-channel imaging (MCI)**, where channels are complementary with minimal overlap. Pure patch masking therefore only learns *intra-channel* structure and fails to exploit cross-channel interactions.

Their fix — **Dynamic Channel-Patch (DCP) masking** — combines:
1. **Random patch masking** with *independently sampled* locations per channel (not one mask replicated across channels).
2. **Dynamic channel masking**: sample the number of channels to mask `k ~ U{0,…,C-1}`, then sample *which* `k` — i.e. **HCS repurposed from a regularizer into a supervision target**. Masked channels' patches are not dropped from the loss; they become the reconstruction targets.
3. A mix probability `p_patch, p_channel` to choose patch-masking vs channel-masking per step.

This unifies the "channel-subset regularization" already in your spec with the pretraining objective: **you get the cross-panel robustness regularizer and the representation-learning signal from the same masking procedure.**

Their results on **CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, So2Sat**: +3.0–21.5% over SOTA MCI-ViTs, and it directly yields **robustness to varying channel configurations** at inference.

Corroborating evidence that channel masking is the point:
- **MIM-CyCIF** (Sims et al., *Commun. Biol.* 2024; PMLR v240) — channel-wise masking of 25 CyCIF markers, single-cell images reshaped so each "patch" is one channel; the MAE objective becomes **marker imputation / panel reduction** directly.
- **CA-MAE** (Recursion, CVPR 2024) — channel-agnostic MAE that generalizes across channel counts/orders, pretrained on RPI-93M, evaluated zero-shot-ish on JUMP-CP with a *different* channel structure. Code: `github.com/recursionpharma/maes_microscopy`.
- **ChannelMAE** (`github.com/saiprabhakar/ChannelMAE`) — a direct MAE + ChannelViT fusion; `models_chamae.py`.
- **SatMAE** group-channel variant — shows the same pattern works for grouped channels (`spatial_mask` toggle: mask a spatial location across all channels vs. independently per channel).
- **VirTues** (bio.rodeo) — full MAE where "fully masked channels can be inpainted," i.e. **virtual staining as a pretraining byproduct**.

---

## 3. The architectural tension you must resolve: fusion bottleneck vs. reconstruction fidelity

The single-query cross-attention collapses `C → k` vectors. For MAE you must reconstruct the *masked channels' raw pixels* from that joint embedding. If `k=1`, you're training a `C → 1 → C` autoencoder — the bottleneck may be too lossy to give a strong reconstruction gradient (kills the SSL signal), or too lossy to preserve per-channel detail.

Resolutions (in increasing order of preference):

1. **Increase `k`** (multi-query PMA). Modest, easy. But it dilutes the fixed-size-representation virtue if `k` grows with `C`.
2. **Add memory / register tokens** — this is **ChA-MAEViT's** explicit remedy: learnable tokens carried through *both* encoder and decoder "as long-term memory to retain key cross-channel information," addressing "structurally diverse channels" that can't be reconstructed from each other. Keep them fixed-count and independent of `C`.
3. **Keep channel tokens alive through the encoder** (not fully collapsed before the decoder). ChA-MAEViT argues against fully pre-collapsing; a **Channel-Aware Decoder**, shared across all channels (scales to 18+ channels; per-channel decoders do not), consumes per-channel tokens + memory tokens. Note this slightly weakens the "fuse before the spatial transformer" compute argument — a reasonable tradeoff is: **fuse for the *representation* path, but expose the unmasked channel tokens to the light decoder** for reconstruction.
4. **Factorized marker × spatial attention** — **VirTues** splits attention into a marker axis and a spatial axis rather than joint, explicitly "avoiding the quadratic blow-up that makes standard ViTs impractical on high-plex imaging." This is the cleanest way to keep both per-channel fidelity and bounded compute, and it composes with your varlen padding-free path on each axis.

Recommendation: **k=1 fixed query for the pretrained representation output, plus fixed-count memory tokens, plus a shared channel-aware decoder that can also see the unmasked channel tokens.** Validate against the multi-query variant.

---

## 4. Decoder must be conditioned on channel identity

When reconstructing a masked channel, the decoder must know **which** marker it's reconstructing. Your **additive channel-identity embedding** (learnable marker ID or text-conditioned) is not just for the encoder — feed the target channel's identity vector to the decoder as well. This turns the identity embedding into a **target specification** and is what lets one shared decoder handle all channels:

> ChA-MAEViT: "a shared lightweight decoder utilizes channel tokens to provide channel-specific behavior."

This also sets up open-vocabulary nicely (§6).

---

## 5. Loss

Per-channel **normalized pixel loss** over masked patches (standard MAE normalizes per patch; for MCI normalize **per channel** so heterogeneous intensity ranges don't bias the objective). ChA-MAEViT reports Spearman correlation of mean intensity + SSIM as the HCI-relevant reconstruction metrics.

---

## 6. Novel / unseen channels — now a strength

Because your identity embeddings can be **text-conditioned** (PhenoPLIFT-style), you get a route to zero-shot identity that ChA-MAEViT had to approximate: they initialize new channel tokens randomly and **fine-tune only the channel tokens (rest frozen) using the reconstruction loss on a few unlabeled test images** — improving novel-channel accuracy from 9.2% to 11.6% with 640 unlabeled images. Text-conditioned identity should beat random init *before* any fine-tuning, and VirTues demonstrates the stronger version: **sequence-grounded marker tokens (ESM-2 embeddings of the protein's UniProt sequence) fused with image content**, giving "zero-shot transfer across panels and platforms," including technologies never seen in pretraining.

If your channels carry a protein/marker name, wiring an ESM-2 embedding in as the identity vector is the single highest-leverage upgrade to your identity path.

---

## 7. What MAE buys you on this backbone (HCI downstream payoffs)

- **Virtual staining / marker imputation as a free byproduct** — masked-channel reconstruction *is* imputation (MIM-CyCIF, miniMTI, VirTues, "Language of Stains").
- **Panel reduction** — use reconstruction fidelity to rank marker subsets (iterative panel selection in MIM-CyCIF / miniMTI).
- **Cross-panel / cross-technology transfer** — CA-MAE and VirTues both demonstrate generalization to unseen channel structures.
- **Stronger than weakly-supervised** — Recursion's CA-MAE reports up to **+11.5% relative** improvement recalling curated biological relationships vs. weak supervision.

---

## 8. Deltas to add to the handoff spec

**Additions to §2 (design):**
- Two masking axes: **spatial patch masking** (independently sampled per channel) + **dynamic channel masking** (HCS-style: sample `k`, then the subset). Mix via `p_patch, p_channel`.
- **Fixed-count memory/register tokens** through encoder + decoder (cardinality-independent — does not break padding-free).
- **Channel-aware shared decoder** (one decoder, not per-channel), optionally fed the unmasked channel tokens + memory tokens.

**Additions to §3 (padding-free):**
- Masking = **token omission** in the varlen tensor (spatial mask drops patch rows; channel mask drops channel rows). No mask tokens, no attention masks for masking.
- Guard: never mask *all* channels (keep ≥1 visible) unless doing pure spatial-only steps.

**Additions to §4 (HCI requirements):**
- Identity embedding is reused **as decoder target conditioning**.
- Optionally replace learnable marker embeddings with **sequence-grounded (ESM-2) identity vectors** for zero-shot new-marker transfer.
- Explicit "novel-channel" protocol: freeze model, adapt only identity vectors via reconstruction loss on a few unlabeled images.

**Additions to §5 (acceptance criteria):**
- [ ] Channel-masked reconstruction: masked-channel output achieves target Spearman/SSIM on a held-out panel; visibly beats spatial-only masking ablation.
- [ ] DCP vs. patch-only ablation reproduced (expect a large gap on MCI, per ChA-MAEViT).
- [ ] Memory-token ablation: removing them degrades masked-channel reconstruction.
- [ ] Zero-shot novel-channel: text/sequence-conditioned identity gives usable reconstruction **without** fine-tuning; report the fine-tuned-tokens upper bound.
- [ ] Padding-free property preserved under masking: encoder input length == number of *visible* tokens; assert no mask/pad tokens exist anywhere.
- [ ] Downstream linprobe transfer to a different-panel dataset.

**Pitfalls (add to §6):**
- **Do not** use patch-only masking as the primary objective — the HCI evidence says cross-channel learning won't happen.
- **Do not** fully collapse channels before the decoder — reconstruction fidelity collapses with it (add memory tokens / expose channel tokens).
- **Do not** use per-channel decoders — doesn't scale past a handful of channels.

---

**Bottom line:** Yes. Train it as a **channel-aware MAE** — padding-free token-drop for spatial masking, HCS-style dynamic channel masking as an explicit reconstruction target, memory tokens + shared channel-aware decoder conditioned on channel identity. This is the design validated by ChA-MAEViT, CA-MAE, MIM-CyCIF, and VirTues, and it turns your missing-channel robustness, open-vocabulary identity, and virtual-staining/imputation capabilities into things the pretraining objective *produces* rather than things you bolt on.
